column1: # Book 6 review (Fable, 2026-10-30). No findings. Secondary 6.1012 accepted: quod dicitur esse alienum is a relative clause (the thing that is called strange), not a concession. Error found on the full read: 6.1121-1122, where repit, conturbat and coactat are singular, the hostile air creeping like mist and cloud (Opus had the mist and cloud as subject). 6.1109 "the black generations of men, their color baked through" as at 6.722. Register: consimili ratione = on a like principle at 6.1131; corpuscula = small bodies (6.1063). Band: 6.1006-1008, 6.1014, 6.1017, 6.1029, 6.1051, 6.1054, 6.1063, 6.1077, 6.1083, 6.1085, 6.1090, 6.1095-1096, 6.1118, 6.1126.

column2: in the middle is emptied, at once the iron's first-beginnings
slip forward into the void and fall, joined, and so it happens
that the ring itself follows, and so goes with its whole body.
So it is less a wonder, the thing that is called strange, {{NOTE: The text of this line is uncertain; the sense is that the result follows naturally from what has just been said.}}
cannot go into the void without the ring itself following;
The same happens in every direction: wherever a place
but at such a time it happens that it pushes the iron on,
the stone's current comes after, and finds everything full
the iron's texture; and in this way it spits from itself
when it has taken in some small bodies of bronze, then it happens
not if the whole sea wished to wash it out with all its waves.
but it is better to grasp many things briefly, in few words.
that hollows meet solids, the hollows of this the solids of that,
Now what the principle of disease is, and from where, suddenly,
a force of sickness, risen, can blow up a deadly disaster
and that, on the other hand, many that make for disease and death
must fly about; when these by chance have happened to rise
to the black generations of men, their color baked through?
and limb, another to another; the varying air does this.
like mist and cloud it creeps little by little, and all
that it passes through it confounds, and forces to change,
either falls on the waters, or settles on the crops themselves,
On a like principle, pestilence often comes on oxen too,
